title: Faith and Human Flourishing: Why Religion Matters More Than Ever for Young Americans
gist: Jenet Erickson and W. Justin Dyer analyze the U.S. sample of the Harvard/Baylor Global Flourishing Study and find religious affiliation remains a strong predictor of flourishing on every domain except financial stability, for men, women and young adults, despite U.S. Christian identification falling from 90% (1972) to 63% (2024). They argue faith communities supply the social capital younger cohorts can no longer get for free, linking religiosity to marriage and family formation.

themes.theme: Global Flourishing Study: religious flourishing gap

insights.claim: The Global Flourishing Study by Harvard's Human Flourishing Program and Baylor's Institute for Studies of Religion is a longitudinal survey of over 200,000 participants in 22 countries measuring six domains of well-being.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A large new longitudinal dataset that will drive a wave of well-being research and policy arguments.

insights.claim: In the U.S. sample of the Global Flourishing Study, religious individuals from almost every religious group reported significantly higher overall flourishing and higher scores in every domain except financial and material stability.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Religiosity correlates with well-being but not with material advantage, suggesting non-economic drivers of flourishing.
insights.quote: They also reported significantly higher flourishing on every single life domain except financial and material stability.

themes.theme: Social capital deficit of Millennials and Zoomers

insights.claim: Older generations inherited a free stock of social capital (trusted neighbors, functional schools, courtship culture, predictable careers) that has become expensive or unattainable for younger cohorts, explaining their lower well-being.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Frames youth malaise as an institutional/social-capital problem rather than an income problem.

insights.claim: Religious communities generate social capital (support, belonging, shared values, trust, meaning) that guides young adults along pathways of family, education and work, filling the gap left by eroded civic institutions.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Faith institutions act as a substitute provider of social infrastructure; their decline has second-order effects on family formation.
insights.quote: Religious participation in a faith community opens up the mechanisms for social capital that makes flourishing possible—support, belonging, shared values, trust, and meaning.
